reliability_codes.A: Completely reliable — authoritative primary / first-party source (a national CERT for its own jurisdiction, a vendor PSIRT for its own products); no history of error.
reliability_codes.B: Usually reliable — original research or reporting with consistent editorial standards and only minor, infrequent issues (most reputable research labs; large corroborating outlets).
reliability_codes.C: Fairly reliable — some doubt about consistency, OR the source mainly aggregates / re-reports rather than originates. Corroborate before acting.
reliability_codes.D: Not usually reliable — significant doubt; carries unverified claims but has occasionally been valid.
reliability_codes.E: Unreliable — history of invalid information or propaganda.
reliability_codes.F: Reliability cannot be judged — no track record to evaluate.

tiers.essential: Queried on EVERY daily run (national CERTs / NCSC / CISA / ENISA-class authorities + exploitation ground truth). A daily run that did not attempt one of these is a coverage defect the run must disclose.
tiers.standard: Rotation pool — allocated to sub-agents by staleness (oldest last_successful_fetch first) so every source is attempted at least every ~7 runs; balanced, nothing silently starves.

statuses.candidate: Proposed by an earlier run; awaiting human review before activation
statuses.demoted: Lowered reliability or paused after consecutive failed fetches; awaiting human review

fetch_methods._ladder: Best-content-first fetch ladder — always try in this order and ALWAYS keep a backup transport: (1) rss — structured, dated, carries outbound links; (2) webfetch — Claude's WebFetch tool; (3) jina — the r.jina.ai reader proxy (clean markdown, server-side egress bypasses anti-bot/WAF/geo blocks and runs page JS); (4) bridge/api — dedicated fetch_source.py recipe (browser UA / publisher API). A record's `fetch_method` names the PRIMARY transport; the reader (jina) is the universal fallback available to every method, and `fetch_source.py url` auto-falls-back to it. `blocked` is reserved for content unreachable by every transport including the reader.
fetch_methods.rss: PREFERRED where a feed exists. Use the documented RSS/Atom URL (`rss_url`, else the record's notes) via `python3 tools/fetch_source.py feed <URL> [N]` — many sites are JS-rendered SPAs whose listing page is empty to WebFetch but whose feed is plain XML. `feed` auto-falls-back to the reader if the direct feed GET is WAF-blocked. Then drill each item `link` for the body.
fetch_methods.webfetch: Claude Code's WebFetch tool fetches with its routine User-Agent and a small AI summarisation pass (append the outbound-links template). Works on most publishers. On a 403 / anti-bot / JS-shell, escalate to `jina` then `bridge`.
fetch_methods.jina: Fetch through the r.jina.ai reader proxy: `python3 tools/fetch_source.py jina <URL>` (clean markdown; `jina <URL> html` for simplified HTML). The reader fetches from its OWN egress and executes page JS, so it bypasses anti-bot / WAF / geo blocks (Cloudflare, Akamai, geo-gates) and hydrates SPAs. The primary transport for hosts that block our egress directly but the reader reaches.
fetch_methods.bridge: Use `python3 tools/fetch_source.py <recipe>` (browser User-Agent, no auth) for publishers that 403 the routine UA or serve a JS-only shell. No host allowlist — works on any HTTPS host (layer-3 SSRF defences apply); many hosts have a dedicated subcommand (cisa page/feed/csaf, ncsc-csh, enisa-euvd, bsi-csaf, msrc, osv, feed, url, …). The generic `url <URL>` auto-falls-back to the jina reader on a challenge/403.
fetch_methods.api: Bridge-fetcher subcommand for a structured endpoint (e.g. cisa-kev JSON, ncsc-csh dashboard/detail, osv vuln/query, msrc). Returns parsed JSON.
fetch_methods.blocked: Unreachable by EVERY transport — direct fetch, the jina reader, AND the bridge all fail (e.g. coe.int / downloads.seppmail.com return 401 even to the reader). Surface as a coverage gap and WebSearch for a corroborating publisher — do not retry.
